title: Address Allocation for Private Internets
organization: Cisco Systems / Chrysler Corp. / RIPE NCC

hero.subtitle: Defining the three private IPv4 address ranges used worldwide

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1918 addresses one of the most pressing challenges of the early Internet: IPv4 address exhaustion. By reserving three blocks of the IP address space for private networks, this document enabled organizations to use IP internally without consuming globally unique addresses.

The private address ranges defined in this RFC are the foundation of virtually every home and enterprise network in the world. Combined with Network Address Translation (NAT), they have extended the life of IPv4 far beyond original predictions.

sections.title: Private Address Ranges
sections.content:
The Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) has reserved the following three blocks of the IP address space for private internets:

10.0.0.0/810.0.0.0 - 10.255.255.255 (Class A)16,777,216 hosts
172.16.0.0/12172.16.0.0 - 172.31.255.255 (Class B)1,048,576 hosts
192.168.0.0/16192.168.0.0 - 192.168.255.255 (Class C)65,536 hosts

An enterprise that decides to use IP addresses from these ranges can do so without coordination with IANA or any Internet registry. These addresses are guaranteed to never be assigned as globally unique addresses.

sections.title: Motivation
sections.content:
Many enterprises need network connectivity for internal communications but do not require full external Internet access from every host. Using private addresses for such hosts conserves globally unique addresses.

Address Conservation
The IPv4 address space is limited to approximately 4.3 billion addresses. Private addressing dramatically reduces demand for globally unique allocations.
Network Isolation
Hosts using private addresses cannot be directly reached from the public Internet, providing a natural layer of security through obscurity.
Flexible Allocation
Organizations can freely assign and restructure private addresses without external coordination, simplifying network management.

sections.title: Routing Considerations
sections.content:
Internet routers MUST NOT forward traffic with source or destination addresses in the private ranges. These addresses are non-routable by definition on the public Internet.

ISPs and backbone operators SHOULD filter private addresses at their borders. Leaking private address routes into the global routing table causes black-holing of traffic and routing instability.

For hosts that need connectivity beyond their private network, Network Address Translation (NAT) or application-layer gateways must be deployed at the boundary between the private network and the public Internet.

sections.title: DNS Issues
sections.content:
Private addresses create challenges for DNS. Private network information (such as address-to-name mappings) should not leak into the public DNS infrastructure.

Split DNS
Organizations commonly deploy split DNS, where internal resolvers return private addresses for internal queries while external DNS shows only public addresses.
Reverse DNS
Reverse lookups for private addresses (e.g., 10.in-addr.arpa) should be handled locally and never forwarded to the public DNS hierarchy.

RFC 6303 later formalized the requirement for DNS servers to handle reverse zones for private addresses locally, preventing unnecessary queries to the root and authoritative servers.
